role: Budget model benchmark results (B4), generated by models/tools/budget/test_benchmarks.py; do not edit by hand.

benchmarks.name: The baseline equals CBO's February 2026 projections plus the documented adjustments
benchmarks.tolerance: exact (the file's three decimals; the unrounded values are the same floating-point numbers)
benchmarks.source: CBO, *The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036* and *The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056* (February 2026), from CBO's data files; the FY2026 actuals and the ADJ-T1 and ADJ-T2 tariff adjustments in models/data/budget/post-february.csv
benchmarks.why: B2's test (models/tools/budget/test_data.py, class Reproduction, run-all step 5b) rebuilds the adopted baseline from the data layer alone. This benchmark runs that test and reports it; it does not repeat it. One baseline, reproduced exactly, is the foundation every other figure stands on.

benchmarks.name: Deficit equals outlays minus revenue, every year and scenario
benchmarks.source: Accounting definition (CBO's deficit is total outlays less total revenues)
benchmarks.why: The fiscal model builds the deficit from its parts in two places; they must agree to rounding error. Checked for all 10 scenarios, FY2026-2056.

benchmarks.name: The program's added debt grows by exactly its added deficit (spending, revenue and interest)
benchmarks.source: Accounting definition: debt(t) = debt(t-1) + deficit(t) + other means of financing; the program has no other means of financing
benchmarks.why: Checked on both bases (unified and general fund) for every scenario. The program's debt is what decides the D4 guardrails, so it must not leak or gain anything outside its own deficits.

benchmarks.name: Debt held by the public: the residual after deficits is CBO's own other means of financing, in every scenario
benchmarks.source: CBO February 2026 ten-year and long-term projections of debt and deficits, as stored in the adopted baseline (models/data/fiscal-baseline.csv, to $1 million)
benchmarks.why: CBO's debt grows by more or less than its deficits because of other means of financing (mainly the cash flows of federal credit programs such as student loans). The model takes CBO's debt path, so it carries that residual. The test is that the residual is exactly CBO's, FY2027-2056, in every scenario: the tariff adjustments, the program and the interest-rate cases add none.
detail: The residual itself (reported, not tested): -349 billion in total over FY2027-36; largest single year 2035, -69.7 billion. FY2026 is left out because its debt is the preliminary actual (models/data/budget/post-february.csv). The model carries the gap between that actual and CBO's projection for FY2026 (+305 billion) into every later year, with interest, as a deficit, not as other financing; so CBO's FY2027 residual is measured from CBO's own FY2026 projection.

benchmarks.name: Interest on the program's borrowing follows from its debt and the stated rates
benchmarks.source: The model's stated rate rules, CONVENTIONS.md section 10: ASM-RATE-MARGINAL, ASM-RATE-LT, ASM-RATE-HALFYEAR, ASM-RATE-SHIFT; CBO's February 2026 rates (3-month bill, 10-year note, average rate on debt)
benchmarks.why: Recomputed here from the written rules, independently of fiscal-model.py's code: interest = rate x last year's added debt + rate x half of this year's added deficit, at the higher of CBO's average rate and a 40/60 bill-note blend through 2036 and the baseline's implied rate after, plus one point from 2030 in the R1 cases.

benchmarks.name: The baseline's net interest is consistent with its debt and CBO's average interest rate
benchmarks.tolerance: 0.25 percentage point in every year FY2027-36
benchmarks.source: CBO February 2026 ten-year file: net interest, debt held by the public, average interest rate on debt
benchmarks.why: Net interest divided by last year's debt (the implied rate) should sit close to CBO's own average rate. They differ by definition: CBO's rate is on debt held by the public averaged over the year, while net interest also nets other interest paid and received, and last year's debt is lower than the year's average. A quarter point allows for that and would still catch a units or year-alignment error.
detail: Largest gap in FY2036: implied 4.04%, CBO 3.939%.

benchmarks.name: Nominal equals real times the deflator, and share of GDP times GDP (B2's two conversions)
benchmarks.source: models/data/budget/deflators.csv (CBO's CPI-U and GDP price index) and the baseline's GDP; data.to_real and data.to_pct_gdp
benchmarks.why: Every real-dollar and share-of-GDP figure must come back to the same nominal dollars. Checked on total outlays, FY1962-2056, for both price indexes and two base years.

benchmarks.name: JCT: extending P.L. 119-21's four household deductions; the library's timing of a permanent revenue provision
benchmarks.source: JCT estimates in CBO's letter of August 4, 2025 (publication 61466, SRC-1093), Table 2, from the PDF in Espen's November 8 upload (PR #121)
benchmarks.why: The library doesn't estimate how much a provision costs: it takes a total and spreads it over the years. So the test of the library is the spreading. The FY2030-34 total JCT gives ($351 billion) goes in; the library's method (provisions.profile_path) with the project's default spec for a revenue row (full from the start, growing with individual income tax receipts, permanent: ASM-PROF-REVENUE) puts out the yearly amounts, compared with JCT's in every year. Five percent allows for JCT's rounding to the billion and the different baseline (January 2025). Over a five-year window it can't tell growth rates apart by less than about two points a year, so the growth gap below is reported as a finding, not tested.
detail: Largest yearly gap: FY2030, -4.5%.

JCT's amounts grow about 1.8% a year, FY2030-34; the default spec grows 4.0% a year, the speed of individual income tax receipts. A likely reason: the deductions are fixed dollar amounts ($25,000 of tips, $12,500 of overtime, $10,000 of car-loan interest, $6,000 for each senior), so their cost would grow more slowly than the tax base; whether the statute indexes them was not checked here. For a provision like this the default spec front-loads too little and back-loads too much.
For comparison only (not the test): the same spec growing with CPI-U gives FY2030 67.1 and FY2034 73.4.

benchmarks.name: CBO: interest cost of extending P.L. 119-21's ten temporary provisions, FY2025-34
benchmarks.source: CBO's letter of August 4, 2025 (publication 61466, SRC-1093): debt service $789 billion with the extension, $718 billion without; Table 2 for the deficits, every year FY2029-34; from the PDF in Espen's November 8 upload (PR #121)
benchmarks.why: Tests the model's interest method (fiscal-model.py, debt_roll: market rates on new borrowing, half a year of interest on each year's new deficit) against CBO's own debt-service estimate for the same deficits. JCT's deficits go in, year by year; the model's interest comes out. Fifteen percent allows for one known difference: CBO used its January 2025 interest rates and the model uses February 2026's. (Until the PDF arrived, FY2031-33 were set equal; Table 2's own years now go in.)
detail: The model is +13% from CBO. A higher figure is the cautious direction: the model's rate on new borrowing is at least the market blend.

Table 2 gives the debt service only for the act and the extension together (by year: FY2026 14 rising to FY2034 155), so the extension's own $71 billion is CBO's two totals differenced, not a yearly series.

benchmarks.name: CBO: discretionary defense outlays from budget authority (February 2026 baseline)
benchmarks.source: CBO February 2026 baseline by budget account (US-CBO/cbo-data spending_detail, models/data/budget/cbo-spending-by-function.csv)
benchmarks.why: Tests B3's spend-out method (provisions.cbo_discretionary_outlays, on B2's CBO-calibrated shares, ASM-SPENDOUT) against CBO's own conversion of budget authority into outlays: CBO's projected discretionary defense budget authority, account by account, goes in; outlays FY2029-2036 come out. Five percent in each year is about twice the fit error of B2's historical timing (2.2% of mean outlays), so it allows for the fit and would catch a wrong rate. **This is partly in-sample.** B2 set the shares' overall level (one scale factor, 1.009) so that, over these same years, they give CBO's outlays. So the total is fitted, not tested; what is tested is the year-by-year timing, which comes from OMB's history (FY1993-2019), not from CBO.
detail: Over FY2029-2036 the method gives -0.01% of CBO's total (fitted). Largest year FY2035: 1077 against CBO's 1068 billion.

benchmarks.name: CBO: discretionary nondefense outlays from budget authority (February 2026 baseline)
benchmarks.source: CBO February 2026 baseline by budget account (US-CBO/cbo-data spending_detail, models/data/budget/cbo-spending-by-function.csv)
benchmarks.why: Tests B3's spend-out method (provisions.cbo_discretionary_outlays, on B2's CBO-calibrated shares, ASM-SPENDOUT) against CBO's own conversion of budget authority into outlays: CBO's projected discretionary nondefense budget authority, account by account, goes in; outlays FY2029-2036 come out, with the outlays of accounts that have no discretionary budget authority added separately. Five percent in each year is about twice the fit error of B2's historical timing (3.3% after ground transportation is set aside of mean outlays), so it allows for the fit and would catch a wrong rate. **This is partly in-sample.** B2 set the shares' overall level (one scale factor, 0.998) so that, over these same years, they give CBO's outlays. So the total is fitted, not tested; what is tested is the year-by-year timing, which comes from OMB's history (FY1993-2019), not from CBO.
detail: Over FY2029-2036 the method gives +0.00% of CBO's total (fitted). Largest year FY2029: 996 against CBO's 1010 billion.

Earlier reading (#113): before B3's fix (#118), the library rescaled B2's OMB-fit nondefense shares, which add to 1.10, down to one, and added nothing for highway and transit. That fell 11.1% short in FY2029 and failed. With B2's OMB-fit shares as stored, the FY2029 gap was -2.6%: the extra tenth stood in for outlays whose budget authority isn't discretionary (B2 measured about $94 billion a year, $87 billion of it in function 400: highways, transit, airports). #118 now carries those outlays on their own, which is what this benchmark reads.

benchmarks.name: CBO: outlays by year from one appropriations act's new defense budget authority (2024 Israel security supplemental, Title I, Defense)
benchmarks.tolerance: within 10 points of CBO's cumulative share in each of the first four years
benchmarks.source: CBO, Estimated Budgetary Effects of the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024 (November 1, 2023; SRC-1170), fetched from cbo.gov on November 8, 2026 through a search tool, as Espen allowed that day
benchmarks.why: Tests the library's spend-out (provisions.spendout_apply, on B2's CBO-calibrated defense shares, ASM-SPENDOUT) on a single act: one year of new budget authority goes in, and the share spent by the end of each year comes out, against CBO's own estimate for the same money. Cumulative shares measure timing without depending on the act's size. Ten points allows for one act differing from the average pattern the shares are fit to; a bigger gap means the library would misplace that kind of spending by a year or more.
detail: This is one emergency supplemental, not a regular appropriation. The library uses one set of shares for every defense row, fit to the average of all such spending; a single act's programs can spend much faster or slower. The result shows how far one act can sit from that average, which is a limit on the library's per-row timing rather than proof that the average is wrong (PS-3 tests the average).
The library's defense shares spend 103% of the money by the end of year 3 and take some back in year 4, because B2's year-4 defense share is negative and is used as stored (ASM-SPENDOUT-NORM).
The two FY2026 House estimates Espen uploaded (H.R. 6938, H.R. 7006) were checked first: they report FY2026 only, with prior years' appropriations mixed into the outlays, so they can't test timing.

benchmarks.name: CBO: outlays by year from one appropriations act's new nondefense budget authority (2024 Israel security supplemental, Title II, State, Foreign Operations)
benchmarks.tolerance: within 10 points of CBO's cumulative share in each of the first four years
benchmarks.source: CBO, Estimated Budgetary Effects of the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024 (November 1, 2023; SRC-1170), fetched from cbo.gov on November 8, 2026 through a search tool, as Espen allowed that day
benchmarks.why: Tests the library's spend-out (provisions.spendout_apply, on B2's CBO-calibrated nondefense shares, ASM-SPENDOUT) on a single act: one year of new budget authority goes in, and the share spent by the end of each year comes out, against CBO's own estimate for the same money. Cumulative shares measure timing without depending on the act's size. Ten points allows for one act differing from the average pattern the shares are fit to; a bigger gap means the library would misplace that kind of spending by a year or more.
detail: CBO by year (millions): 3583, 60, 33, 15, 5, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0 from $3,700 million.

This is one emergency supplemental, not a regular appropriation. The library uses one set of shares for every nondefense row, fit to the average of all such spending; a single act's programs can spend much faster or slower. The result shows how far one act can sit from that average, which is a limit on the library's per-row timing rather than proof that the average is wrong (PS-3 tests the average).
The library's shares spend the money evenly over four years; CBO spends this act's almost at once.
The two FY2026 House estimates Espen uploaded (H.R. 6938, H.R. 7006) were checked first: they report FY2026 only, with prior years' appropriations mixed into the outlays, so they can't test timing.

benchmarks.name: Interest rates 0.1 point higher on all debt from FY2026: added net interest
benchmarks.tolerance: ten-year total within 15%, and each year within 25%
benchmarks.source: CBO, How Changes in Economic Conditions Might Affect the Federal Budget: 2026 to 2036 (publication 62257, April 2026), Table 3, on the February 2026 baseline; Espen's November 8 upload (PR #121). Treasury, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt, September 30, 2026, for the maturity structure (models/data/budget/treasury-maturity.csv)
benchmarks.why: The model's stress cases (DEC-R1, BASE-R1) raise every rate by one point from FY2030. Here the same method, rewritten from its written rule and checked to give BASE-R1 to the dollar, is run on CBO's own scenario: every rate 0.1 point higher each year from FY2026, CBO's first year, on the model's baseline. That compares like with like, with no scaling. FY2026 itself is not compared, because the model's FY2026 is the actual year and CBO's FY2026 shock is partial. As in CBO's rules of thumb, the higher rate reaches the debt outstanding at the start only as it is refinanced, on Treasury's maturity structure (ASM-RATE-ROLLOVER); new borrowing pays it in full. CBO says its rules of thumb are roughly symmetrical and scalable up to one point. The total gets 15% for CBO's rounding and the model's simpler rate rule; each year gets 25%, because the stress case is read year by year (the guardrails in 2035, 2045 and 2056), so timing matters as well as the total. Revenue effects (Federal Reserve remittances, under $5 billion a year in CBO's table) are left out of both sides.
detail: Before B6 the model applied the higher rate to all of last year's debt at once. On this scenario that method gave $517 billion over FY2027-36 and $34 billion in FY2027 (from a FY2027 start, B4's run: $502 billion and $32 billion), against CBO's $383 billion and $14 billion. Phasing the rate in as debt rolls over is B6's fix (item 1).
In the model's own +1 point case (BASE-R1), the phased method adds $95 billion in FY2030, the first year, and $4228 billion over FY2030-39.

Cross-check: CBO's 2025 workbook (61183, January 2025 baseline) gives +13.34 billion in FY2026 for the same scenario. Those are the figures in Espen's old CBO scorer (SRC-0203), so that table came from it.

benchmarks.name: Slower growth (productivity growth 0.1 point a year slower from FY2026): added deficits, FY2027-36
benchmarks.source: CBO, How Changes in Economic Conditions Might Affect the Federal Budget: 2026 to 2036 (publication 62257, April 2026), Tables 1 and 2; Espen's November 8 upload (PR #121); copied into models/data/budget/cbo-rules-of-thumb.csv
benchmarks.why: B6 (item 2) gives the model a growth link (fiscal-model.py, growth_path; ASM-GROWTH-LINK): CBO's own effects on revenue, mandatory spending and interest rates, as shares of GDP by year of the shock, scaled to the size of the change; the model then borrows the added deficits at its own rate. **This is in-sample.** The link is taken from the same CBO table it is checked against, so the benchmark tests only the model's debt service on the added deficits ($43 billion against CBO's $40 billion) and the bookkeeping, not how well the link predicts. Fifteen percent is the same allowance as SE-1's total.
detail: Out of sample, across vintages: the same method calibrated to CBO's 2025 workbook (61183, January 2025 baseline) and applied to the February 2026 baseline gives $421 billion, +33% from CBO's 2026 figure. CBO's own rules of thumb moved that much between the two baselines, mostly through a larger effect of lower interest rates in 2026. Read any growth reading with that much uncertainty.
Not modeled: program rows indexed to GDP would also shrink with slower growth; the link moves the baseline only.

benchmarks.name: Slower growth (labor force growth 0.1 point a year slower from FY2026): added deficits, FY2027-36
benchmarks.source: CBO, How Changes in Economic Conditions Might Affect the Federal Budget: 2026 to 2036 (publication 62257, April 2026), Tables 1 and 2; Espen's November 8 upload (PR #121); copied into models/data/budget/cbo-rules-of-thumb.csv
benchmarks.why: B6 (item 2) gives the model a growth link (fiscal-model.py, growth_path; ASM-GROWTH-LINK): CBO's own effects on revenue, mandatory spending and interest rates, as shares of GDP by year of the shock, scaled to the size of the change; the model then borrows the added deficits at its own rate. **This is in-sample.** The link is taken from the same CBO table it is checked against, so the benchmark tests only the model's debt service on the added deficits ($22 billion against CBO's $20 billion) and the bookkeeping, not how well the link predicts. Fifteen percent is the same allowance as SE-1's total.
detail: Out of sample, across vintages: the same method calibrated to CBO's 2025 workbook (61183, January 2025 baseline) and applied to the February 2026 baseline gives $199 billion, +20% from CBO's 2026 figure. CBO's own rules of thumb moved that much between the two baselines, mostly through a larger effect of lower interest rates in 2026. Read any growth reading with that much uncertainty.
Not modeled: program rows indexed to GDP would also shrink with slower growth; the link moves the baseline only.

benchmarks.name: Social Security (OASDI combined): current law
benchmarks.tolerance: depletion year exact; payable within 1 point; 75-year balance within 0.05 point of taxable payroll
benchmarks.source: 2026 Social Security and Medicare Trustees Reports, intermediate assumptions, as recorded in models/data/inputs/funds-*.csv and printed beside the model's figures by models/tools/funds-model.py (lines 306 and 335; legacy/index/dedicated-funds.md)
benchmarks.why: funds-model.py already runs this check against the Trustees on every run and prints it; this benchmark reads its output (build/funds.json) and applies a stated tolerance. The engine uses the Trustees' own annual rates, so it should land on their figures to within rounding: the tolerances are the published rounding (whole percent payable) plus a small allowance for the balance, which funds-model.py says differs only by "rounding in the published rates and the interest path".

benchmarks.name: Medicare Hospital Insurance: current law
benchmarks.tolerance: depletion year exact; payable within 1 point; 75-year balance within 0.05 point of taxable payroll
benchmarks.miss: depletion +1 year, balance -0.08 points of payroll
benchmarks.source: 2026 Social Security and Medicare Trustees Reports, intermediate assumptions, as recorded in models/data/inputs/funds-*.csv and printed beside the model's figures by models/tools/funds-model.py (lines 306 and 335; legacy/index/dedicated-funds.md)
benchmarks.why: funds-model.py already runs this check against the Trustees on every run and prints it; this benchmark reads its output (build/funds.json) and applies a stated tolerance. The engine uses the Trustees' own annual rates, so it should land on their figures to within rounding: the tolerances are the published rounding (whole percent payable) plus a small allowance for the balance, which funds-model.py says differs only by "rounding in the published rates and the interest path".
detail: funds-model.py's own page says the HI check is off and that the program's gain, not the absolute balance, is the reading to use (legacy/index/dedicated-funds.md, Medicare HI).

Which reference: the Trustees. The engine runs on the Trustees' own cost and income rates, so their projection is the one it should reproduce, and the miss is against them. CBO projects HI exhausted during FY2040 (Long-Term Budget Outlook data, February 2026; Espen's November 8 upload, PR #121), 7 years after the Trustees and 6 after the model. That gap is a difference between the two forecasters' assumptions, not a check on the engine, so it is context, not a target.

benchmarks.name: SSA's own scores of seven Social Security provisions, rebuilt by the engine
benchmarks.tolerance: 0.05 point of taxable payroll for each provision
benchmarks.source: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, single-provision estimates on the 2026 Trustees' basis (models/data/inputs/funds-ss-ssa-runs.csv)
benchmarks.why: funds-model.py rebuilds seven of SSA's own provision scores from the same tax bases it uses for the plan's Social Security provisions. SSA publishes them to 0.01 point; 0.05 allows for that and the engine's fitted tail.
detail: Largest gap: A6: CPI-E COLA from Dec 2028, model -0.349 against SSA -0.33.
